newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean police hunt suspected Northern assassins.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean police hunt suspected Northern assassins.

text.p: South Korean police stepped up a manhunt on Wednesday for two suspected North Korean assassins after the death of a Pyongyang defector who was shot earlier this month, a police official said.

Police are working on the theory that Pyongyang instructed its agents to murder Lee Han-young as a warning to South Korea and other North Korean escapees after the defection of the country's top ideologue on February 15.
Lee was shot in the head and chest near a friend's apartment block in a Seoul suburb three days after Hwang Jang-yop defected to Seoul's consular mission in Beijing.

Talks between South Korea and China over the fate of Hwang could restart later today after being stalled by the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, according to a Seoul official in the Chinese capital.
South Korean police have virtually ruled out the possibility that Lee was gunned down by loan sharks or underworld hitmen, police spokesman Ha Seung-gyun said.
"All the evidence we have points to an act of North Korean spies," Ha said in an interview.

Lee, whose mother is the sister of a former wife of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, ran into financial trouble after he defected to the South in 1982 and went into business. He spent 10 months in jail in 1993 for embezzling funds.
Lee went to great lengths to disguise his real identity, changing his name from Li Il-nam and even undergoing plastic surgery on his face.
Desperate for money, he went public last year with a biography and appeared on a talk show after his mother's defection, reportedly to a Western nation.
"We suspect the gun used was a Belgian-made Browning pistol, which is often used by North Korean agents. The bullet shells found on the scene are the same found in a previous spy incident," Ha said.
Police were preparing to scatter 30,000 leaflets in the suburb of Bundang bearing a computer-enhanced video image of one of the assassins.
One of the suspects was caught by a bank surveillance camera before the shooting. A reward of $140,000 for information on the killing already has been offered.
The black-and-white image shows one of the two suspected attackers, a man in his late twenties or early thirties wearing a half-length overcoat.
Ha said police were relying heavily on citizen's reports to try to crack the case.
Lee survived 10 days in a coma on a life support system after a bullet lodged in his brain, too deeply to be removed. He died of heart failure, hospital officials said.
He is the first defector to be assassinated since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War, according to police.

The shooting has frightened the small community of Pyongyang defectors in Seoul. Some 600 escapees now live in the South, and the celebrities among them have begun surrounding themselves with bodyguards.
Hwang, the Pyongyang ideologue now in Beijing, was reported by South Korean media to have revealed that North Korea has 50,000 agents in the South.
